cases.doctrine: The comparison is not restricted to identical goods. A mark may be refused where the signs are similar and the goods or services are related so that the public may infer a business connection.
cases.examUse: Spot Sec. 123.1(d)(iii): similar signs plus related goods or services can bar registration through likely confusion of business.
cases.facts: IFP applied to register OK Hotdog Inasal Cheese Hotdog Flavor Mark for snack products. Mang Inasal opposed based on its earlier registered MANG INASAL mark for restaurant services, known for chicken inasal.
cases.issue: Was the proposed snack mark similar to the earlier mark, with related goods and services, so that registration was barred by Sec. 123.1(d)(iii)?
cases.keyPhrase: likely to cause deception or confusion
cases.name: Mang Inasal Philippines, Inc. v. IFP Manufacturing Corp.
cases.note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
cases.ruling: The Court granted Mang Inasal's petition, applied the dominancy test, found INASAL dominant, and treated the goods and services as related in the circumstances, creating likely confusion of business.

cases.doctrine: Likelihood of confusion may concern goods or business/source. The dominant feature, ordinary purchaser, relatedness of goods, and normal potential expansion of business matter; actual confusion is not required.
cases.examUse: Frame confusion two ways (goods and business); dominant feature plus related condiments plus business-expansion inference.
cases.facts: Barrio Fiesta applied to register PAPA BOY & DEVICE for lechon sauce. UFC opposed using its earlier PAPA and PAPA KETSARAP marks, including for catsup and related condiments.
cases.issue: Was PAPA BOY & DEVICE confusingly similar to UFC's earlier registered PAPA KETSARAP mark for related food products under Sec. 123.1(d)?
cases.keyPhrase: confusion of goods and of business may likely result
cases.name: UFC Philippines, Inc. v. Barrio Fiesta Manufacturing Corp.
cases.note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
cases.ruling: The Court granted UFC's petition and reinstated the IPO rejection of PAPA BOY, finding PAPA dominant in both marks and catsup and lechon sauce closely related condiments; a purchaser could think PAPA BOY belonged to UFC's PAPA sauce family.

cases.doctrine: Use the dominancy test. The Court expressly abandoned the holistic test for resemblance of marks under the IP Code.
cases.examUse: Cite for the current test (dominancy) and the abandonment of the holistic test; compare visual, aural and connotative impressions of dominant features.
cases.facts: The parties asserted competing KOLIN marks over electronic/electrical goods, requiring the Court to settle the proper resemblance test under the IP Code.
cases.issue: Did the holistic test remain a proper alternative to the dominancy test for trademark resemblance?
cases.keyPhrase: the use of the Holistic Test ... has been abandoned
cases.name: Kolin Electronics Co., Inc. v. Kolin Philippines International, Inc.
cases.note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
cases.ruling: The En Banc Court held the holistic test abandoned and the dominancy test prescribed by the IP Code, comparing dominant features and visual, aural and connotative impressions.

cases.doctrine: Sec. 123.1(e) looks to knowledge among the relevant sector of the public, including knowledge obtained through promotion; it is not limited to recognition by the public at large.
cases.examUse: Cite for well-known marks: relevant-sector knowledge, including promotion-derived knowledge, suffices.
cases.facts: Wilton Dy/Philites applied for PHILITES & LETTER P DEVICE for lighting products. Philips opposed, relying on its PHILIPS mark, recognized as registered and well-known in the Philippines.
cases.issue: Was PHILITES & LETTER P DEVICE confusingly similar to PHILIPS, engaging well-known mark protection under Sec. 123?
cases.name: Dy v. Koninklijke Philips Electronics N.V.
cases.note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition and dismissed the PHILITES application, recognizing PHILIPS as registered and well-known and finding the applied-for sign confusingly similar for the same lighting products.

cases.doctrine: The recurring elements are confusing similarity in the general appearance of the goods and intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor. Intent may be inferred from the circumstances.
cases.examUse: Cite for unfair competition: total commercial presentation plus circumstances showing calculation to deceive and ride on goodwill.
cases.facts: San Miguel Pure Foods sold PUREFOODS FIESTA HAM. Foodsphere sold CDO ham in packaging allegedly copying the earlier product's general appearance and layout.
cases.issue: Did Foodsphere commit unfair competition by adopting likely misleading packaging, though the products bore different word marks?
cases.keyPhrase: intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor
cases.name: San Miguel Pure Foods Co., Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc.
cases.note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
cases.ruling: The Court sustained the unfair-competition finding, focusing on the total commercial presentation and circumstances supporting a calculated deception riding on established goodwill.

cases.doctrine: A term generic or descriptive of a class of institutions is not exclusively appropriable unless secondary meaning is established by evidence.
cases.examUse: Cite for genericity/secondary meaning only; the decision arose in the corporate-name context, not as a direct modern Sec. 165 holding.
cases.facts: Lyceum of the Philippines sought to stop other educational institutions from using Lyceum in their corporate names.
cases.issue: Did Lyceum exclusively own the generic/descriptive word through alleged secondary meaning?
cases.name: Lyceum of the Philippines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals
cases.note: Reviewer paraphrase; decided in the corporate-name context - use for genericity/secondary meaning, not as a direct Sec. 165 holding.
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition: Lyceum commonly denoted educational institutions, petitioner failed to prove sufficiently exclusive use signifying only its school, and the other names were not confusingly similar in their entirety.

cases.doctrine: Comparative only. Use to discuss abstract business methods; Philippine analysis begins with RA 8293 Secs. 21-22.
cases.facts: Applicants sought a U.S. patent for a commodity-market risk-hedging method.
cases.issue: Was the business method patent-eligible, and was machine-or-transformation the exclusive U.S. test?
cases.keyPhrase: machine-or-transformation test is not the exclusive test
cases.name: Bilski v. Kappos
cases.note: U.S. Supreme Court comparative authority; not binding Philippine doctrine.
cases.ruling: The U.S. Supreme Court held machine-or-transformation not exclusive, but the hedging claims abstract and ineligible under U.S. law.

cases.doctrine: Comparative only. Adding generic computing to an abstract business idea does not necessarily produce a technical invention under patent law.
cases.facts: Patents claimed intermediated settlement implemented on a generic computer.
cases.issue: Did generic computer implementation make the abstract settlement idea patent-eligible?
cases.name: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International
cases.note: U.S. Supreme Court comparative authority; not binding Philippine doctrine.
cases.ruling: The U.S. Supreme Court held the claims abstract; generic computer implementation supplied no sufficient inventive concept for eligibility.

cases.doctrine: Comparative only. The Philippine statutory test remains Sec. 26 and Philippine doctrine.
cases.facts: The dispute concerned combining an adjustable automobile pedal with an electronic sensor in light of prior art.
cases.issue: Was the claimed combination obvious under U.S. patent law, and was the lower court's test overly rigid?
cases.keyPhrase: flexible approach to the obviousness question
cases.name: KSR International Co. v. Teleflex Inc.
cases.note: U.S. Supreme Court comparative authority; not binding Philippine doctrine.
cases.ruling: The U.S. Supreme Court rejected a rigid teaching-suggestion-motivation formula for a flexible obviousness inquiry; combining familiar elements by known methods may be obvious if yielding predictable results.

cases.doctrine: Comparative only. Copyright originality is independent creation plus at least a minimal amount of creativity; it is not patent novelty.
cases.facts: The dispute concerned a soccer team logo of simple parallel angled lines forming an arrow plus the cursive word Arrows.
cases.issue: Did the logo show enough original creative authorship for U.S. copyright protection?
cases.keyPhrase: some creative authorship in its delineation or form
cases.name: Muller v. New York Arrows Soccer Team, Inc.
cases.note: U.S. Court of Appeals comparative authority; not binding Philippine doctrine.
cases.ruling: The court affirmed denial of copyright protection for lack of sufficient creative authorship in delineation or form.

cases.doctrine: The decision construed PD 49, not the current RA 8293 wording, and addressed the charge-sufficiency/probable-cause stage. It does not eliminate the prosecution's trial burden.
cases.examUse: Limit carefully: PD 49 disjunctive-reading case at the charging stage; do not overstate as current-law doctrine.
cases.facts: Microsoft alleged Manansala distributed/sold unauthorized software copies; a test purchase and search yielded illicit copies. The criminal complaint was brought under Sec. 29 of then-applicable PD 49.
cases.issue: Could sale/distribution of pirated software support the criminal copyright charge without proof the seller personally reproduced the copies?
cases.name: Microsoft Corporation v. Manansala
cases.note: Reviewer paraphrase: construed PD 49 at the charge/probable-cause stage; do not read as current RA 8293 wording.
cases.ruling: The Court reversed the dismissal: PD 49's listed acts were read disjunctively where a conjunctive reading would be absurd, so unauthorized sale/distribution could be an infringing act.

provisions.explanation: The NPC is attached to the DICT and headed by a Privacy Commissioner (also Chairman), assisted by two Deputy Privacy Commissioners for Data Processing Systems and for Policies and Planning. All are appointed by the President for three-year terms, reappointable for another three years. The Commissioner must be at least 35, of good moral character, unquestionable integrity and known probity, and a recognized IT and data-privacy expert (Secretary rank); Deputies must be recognized ICT and data-privacy experts (Undersecretary rank).

The Commission may establish its own Secretariat with administrative, technical and support services; members are appointed under Civil Service Law. A majority must have served at least five years in a government agency involved in processing personal information (e.g. SSS, GSIS, LTO, BIR, PhilHealth, COMELEC, DFA, DOJ, PhilPost).

NPC functions (a)-(q): ensure PIC compliance; receive complaints, investigate, facilitate ADR settlement, adjudicate, award indemnity and publicize reports (as a collegial body except on amicable settlement); issue cease-and-desist orders and processing bans for national-security/public-interest detriment; compel compliance; monitor government security measures; coordinate policy; publish guides and filing-system directories; recommend prosecution and Sec. 25-29 penalties to the DOJ; review privacy codes; assist and advise; interpret the Act; propose legislation; and coordinate cross-border enforcement.

Key definitions: (f) Information and Communications System (system plus procedures for electronic data); (g) Personal Information (identifies alone or in combination, tangible or not); (h) Personal Information Controller (controls or directs processing; excludes mere instructed performers and personal/family/household activity); (i) Personal Information Processor (qualified outsourced processor); (j) Processing (any lifecycle operation); (k) Privileged Information (privileged under Rules of Court and other laws); (l) Sensitive Personal Information (four statutory categories).

Broad scope: all personal-information types and any involved natural or juridical person, including offshore controllers/processors using Philippine equipment or maintaining a local office/branch/agency (subject to Sec. 5). Exclusions (a)-(g): government position/contract-service/benefit information; journalistic, artistic, literary or research processing; public-authority functions; bank CISA/AMLA compliance information; and foreign-resident data collected under foreign law.

Nothing in the Act amends or repeals RA 53 protection for publishers, editors and duly accredited reporters of general-circulation publications against compelled disclosure of confidential news sources. Not a blanket media exemption.

Extraterritorial application to foreign acts or practices where (a) processing relates to a Philippine citizen or resident, (b) the entity has a Philippine link (processing here; or abroad about citizens/residents with links such as a Philippine contract, central management and control, or a local branch/agency/office/subsidiary whose parent or affiliate accesses the data), and (c) other links such as carrying on business here or collecting/holding data through a Philippine entity.

Cumulative principles of transparency, legitimate purpose and proportionality. Data must be collected for specified, legitimate, declared purposes and compatibly processed; processed fairly and lawfully; accurate, relevant and updated; adequate and not excessive; retained only as necessary; and kept identifiable no longer than necessary (longer historical/statistical/scientific storage only as laid down in law with safeguards). The PIC must implement these principles.

Lawful processing requires no legal prohibition plus at least one basis: (a) consent; (b) contract necessity or requested pre-contract steps; (c) legal-obligation compliance; (d) vital interests including life and health; (e) national emergency, public order and safety, or public-authority functions; or (f) legitimate interests of the PIC or disclosing third party unless overridden by constitutional fundamental rights. Consent is one basis, not the only one.

Default prohibition on processing sensitive and privileged information, except: (a) specific prior consent (all parties for privileged exchanges); (b) existing laws/regulations guaranteeing protection without requiring consent; (c) life-and-health necessity where consent is inexpressible; (d) lawful noncommercial public-organization objectives with statutory safeguards; (e) medical treatment by qualified providers with adequate protection; or (f) legal proceedings, claims, or government/public-authority provision.

A PIC may subcontract processing but stays responsible for safeguards: confidentiality, prevention of unauthorized use, and general legal compliance. The PIP must also comply with the Act and applicable laws.

PICs may invoke privileged communication over privileged information they lawfully control or process; evidence gathered on privileged information is inadmissible subject to existing laws and regulations. Privilege must first exist under another law; Sec. 15 creates none for ordinary data.

Data-subject rights: (a) be informed of processing; (b) be furnished processing details and PIC identity; (c) reasonable access on demand to contents, sources, recipients, manner, reasons, automated processes, dates, and PIC designation; (d) dispute and obtain immediate correction of inaccuracies (unless vexatious/unreasonable), with propagation to recipients; (e) suspend, withdraw or order blocking/removal/destruction on substantial proof of defect, unlawfulness or obsolescence; and (f) indemnification for resulting damages.
Lawful heirs and assigns may invoke the data subject's Sec. 16 rights after death or upon incapacity or inability to exercise them.

Where data is processed electronically in a structured, commonly used format, the data subject may obtain a reusable electronic or structured copy of data undergoing processing. The Commission may specify formats, standards, modalities and transfer procedures. Separate from the Sec. 16 list.

Secs. 16-18 do not apply to research-only scientific/statistical use with no actions or decisions regarding the subject, strict confidentiality and purpose limitation; nor to processing gathered for criminal, administrative or tax-liability investigations.

The PIC must implement reasonable, proportionate organizational, physical and technical measures against unlawful or accidental destruction, alteration, disclosure and processing — covering natural and human dangers, calibrated to data sensitivity, risk, size, best practices and cost. Required components: network safeguards, security policy, vulnerability process, and monitoring with breach response. Third-party processors must implement the same measures; personnel stay bound by confidentiality after service ends. Sec. 20(f): prompt NPC and subject notification on reasonably believed unauthorized acquisition of SPI or identity-fraud-enabling data with likely real risk of serious harm, with prescribed content and limited delay.

The PIC is accountable for Act compliance and must use contractual or other reasonable means to secure comparable protection during third-party processing. The PIC must designate accountable individual(s) and disclose their identity to any data subject on request.

Government-held SPI must be secured, as far as practicable, with the most appropriate ICT-industry standard as recommended by the Commission. Each agency or instrumentality head is responsible for compliance; the Commission monitors and may recommend action toward minimum standards.

On-site/online access to government SPI requires source-agency-head security clearance (except under Commission guidelines). Off-site transport or access requires a submitted request with agency-head approval within two business days (inaction is disapproval), capped at 1,000 records at a time and using the Commission-recognized most secure encryption standard.

Government contracts potentially involving SPI of 1,000 or more individuals oblige the agency to require the contractor and its employees to register their processing system with the Commission and comply with the Act, including Sec. 23, as agencies and employees do.
Unauthorized processing: PI draws 1-3 years and P500,000-P2,000,000; SPI draws 3-6 years and P500,000-P4,000,000.
Unauthorized access due to negligence: PI draws 1-3 years and P500,000-P2,000,000; SPI draws 3-6 years and P500,000-P4,000,000.
Knowing or negligent improper disposal in publicly accessible areas or trash: PI draws 6 months-2 years and P100,000-P500,000; SPI draws 1-3 years and P100,000-P1,000,000.
Processing for purposes unauthorized by the subject, the Act or existing law: PI draws 1 year 6 months-5 years and P500,000-P1,000,000; SPI draws 2-7 years and P500,000-P2,000,000.
Knowing, unlawful system intrusion where PI or SPI is stored: 1-3 years and P500,000-P2,000,000.
A PIC that, knowing of a breach and the Sec. 20(f) duty, intentionally or by omission conceals it or its extent: 1 year 6 months-5 years and P500,000-P1,000,000.
Malicious disclosure: a PIC, PIP or their officials/employees/agents who with malice or bad faith disclose unwarranted or false PI/SPI they obtained: 1 year 6 months-5 years and P500,000-P1,000,000.
Unauthorized disclosure to a third party without consent, outside Sec. 31: PI draws 1-3 years and P500,000-P1,000,000; SPI draws 3-5 years and P500,000-P2,000,000.
A combination or series of Secs. 25-32 acts: 3-6 years and P1,000,000-P5,000,000.

For juridical-person offenders, participating or grossly negligent responsible officers are penalized, and the court may suspend or revoke Act rights. Aliens are deported after serving the penalty. Public officers/employees guilty under Secs. 27-28 may suffer disqualification.
Large-scale: the maximum of the respective scale applies where PI of at least 100 persons is harmed, affected or involved.
Public-officer offenders acting in the exercise of duties suffer accessory disqualification from public office for double the criminal penalty's term.
Restitution for aggrieved parties is governed by the New Civil Code.
A mark is any visible sign capable of distinguishing an enterprise's goods (trademark) or services (service mark), including a stamped or marked container of goods.
Rights in a mark are acquired through registration validly made under the law.

Bars to registration: (a) immoral, deceptive, scandalous or disparaging matter; (b) Philippine or foreign flags, arms or insignia; (c) living-individual identifiers (or a deceased President's widow) without consent; (d) identity with registered or earlier-filed marks for same, related or confusingly similar goods/services; (e)-(f) well-known marks and their translations; (g) misleading marks; (h)-(j) generic, customary or descriptive matter; (k) functional shapes; (l) color alone undefined by form; (m) public-order or morality violations.

The Filipino-or-English application must state the registration request, applicant identity and nationality/domicile/establishment, organizing law, agent, priority and color claims, three-dimensional status, reproductions, transliteration/translation, Nice-classed goods/services, and signature or self-identification.
After the opposition period lapses or opposition is denied, the Office issues the certificate of registration on fee payment, with notice published in the IPO Gazette.
The certificate is prima facie (rebuttable) evidence of registration validity, registrant ownership, and the exclusive right to use the mark for the specified and related goods/services.

Ten-year duration, conditioned on filing a declaration of actual use with evidence (or valid obstacle-based reasons) within one year from the fifth anniversary; otherwise the mark is removed from the Register.
Renewal for successive ten-year periods on fee payment and request filed within six months before expiration, or within six months after on payment of the additional fee.

A person believing he is or will be damaged may petition for cancellation within five years from registration; anytime cancellation lies for genericness, abandonment, fraud or contrariety to the Act, source misrepresentation, or three-plus years of uninterrupted non-use without legitimate reason. The section also allocates jurisdiction over enforcement and cancellation actions.

Non-use is excused only by circumstances independent of the owner's will; lack of funds never excuses. Non-distinctiveness-altering use, class-spanning use, and qualifying related-company or controlled-user use are preserved under the stated conditions.

The registered owner may prevent unauthorized commercial use of identical or similar signs or containers for identical or similar goods/services where confusion is likely; identical signs on identical goods/services presume confusion. Registered well-known marks extend to dissimilar goods/services where use indicates a connection and owner interests are likely damaged.

Infringing conduct: (155.1) unauthorized commercial use of a reproduction, counterfeit, copy or colorable imitation of a registered mark, container or dominant feature in connection with sale, offering, distribution or advertising (including preparatory steps) where confusion, mistake or deception is likely; or (155.2) reproducing or imitating the mark or dominant feature and applying it to commercial labels, packaging or advertising where confusion is likely. Either act infringes regardless of actual sale.

Remedies: damages measured by complainant's lost profit, defendant's actual profit, or a reasonable percentage of gross sales or service value; impounding of sales records during suit; doubling on shown actual intent to mislead or defraud; and injunction on proper showing.

Publicly identified goodwill in goods, business or services is a property right with or without a registered mark. Unfair competition is passing off through deception or bad-faith means, or acts calculated to that result. Deemed acts: confusing general appearance of goods; artifice implying another's services; and false or bad-faith discrediting statements. Secs. 156, 157 and 161 remedies apply mutatis mutandis.

D-01: the syllabus cites this provision under Trade Name, but it defines collective mark - a visible sign designated as such in the application, capable of distinguishing the origin or other common characteristic (including quality) of different enterprises' goods or services used under the registered owner's control. The actual trade-name definition is Sec. 121.3; verify against RA 8293.
A trade name is the name or designation identifying or distinguishing an enterprise - the enterprise itself, not a particular product.

A name or designation contrary to public order or morals, particularly one liable to deceive trade circles or the public about the nature of the identified enterprise, may not be used as a trade name.

Trade names are protected even before or without registration; confusing subsequent use as a trade name, mark or collective mark is unlawful. Secs. 153-156 and 166-167 remedies apply mutatis mutandis. Ownership transfers only with the enterprise or relevant part, with Secs. 149.2-149.4 applying mutatis mutandis.
A technical solution of a problem in any field that is new, involves an inventive step and is industrially applicable is patentable, whether a product, process or improvement.

Excluded subject matter: (22.1) discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods; (22.2) mental-act, game or business schemes and computer programs; (22.3) surgical, therapeutic and diagnostic methods (not their products); (22.4) plant varieties, animal breeds, essentially biological processes (not micro-organisms or microbiological processes); (22.5) aesthetic creations; (22.6) public-order or morality violations.
Utility models require novelty and industrial applicability; Sec. 21 applies except for inventive step, which is not a condition.

An industrial design is any composition of lines or colors or three-dimensional form giving a special appearance to and serving as pattern for an industrial product or handicraft - appearance, not function.
Only new or original designs are protected; purely technical or functional shapes and designs contrary to public order, health or morals are excluded.
An invention forming part of prior art is not new.

Prior art is everything publicly available worldwide before the filing or priority date, plus the contents of qualifying earlier-filed published Philippine patent, utility-model or design applications, subject to the section's conditions.
Twelve-month grace: pre-filing disclosures by the inventor, by a patent office in specified circumstances, or by third parties deriving from the inventor do not prejudice novelty.
An invention involves an inventive step if, given prior art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art at the filing or priority date.
An invention producible and usable in any industry is industrially applicable.
The patent right belongs to the inventor, heirs or assigns; joint makers own jointly.
First-to-file: among independent makers of the same invention, the right belongs to the filer with the earliest filing or priority date.

Commissioned inventions belong to the commissioner absent contrary contract. Employee inventions belong to the employee where inventive activity is outside regular duties (even with employer resources), and to the employer where they result from regularly assigned duties, absent contrary agreement.

Reciprocity-based priority: a local application expressly claiming priority, filed within twelve months of the foreign filing, with a certified foreign copy and English translation within six months of Philippine filing, is treated as filed on the foreign date.

One adjudged owner of the patent right may, within three months after finality, prosecute the application, file anew, request refusal, or seek cancellation. One adjudged the true inventor may be substituted as patentee or elect cancellation, with damages if warranted.

The Filipino-or-English application contains the grant request, description, necessary drawings, claims and abstract; no patent issues without inventor identification. Claims define the protection scope.
The filing date is the Office's receipt date of at least an express or implied Philippine-patent request, applicant identification, and a Filipino-or-English description with claims.
Compliant, fee-paid applications are granted, effective on IPO Gazette publication of the grant. Final examiner refusals are appealable to the Director under the Act and Regulations.
Patent term: twenty years from the application filing date.
Interested persons may seek full or partial cancellation for non-patentability, insufficient enabling disclosure, or public-order/morality contrariety.

Utility models expire without renewal seven years after filing. Cancellation lies for disqualification, registration-requirement failure, insufficient description or claims, missing drawings, or non-inventor ownership.

Industrial designs run five years from filing, renewable for at most two consecutive five-year periods. Cancellation lies for non-registrability, lack of novelty, or added subject matter, in full or in part.

Product patents exclude unauthorized making, using, offering, selling or importing; process patents exclude unauthorized process use and dealings in directly or indirectly obtained products. Owners may assign, transmit by succession, and license.
First sale/exhaustion: use of a patented product put on the Philippine market by or with the owner's express consent is beyond the owner's control after that marketing.
Further limits: qualifying private non-commercial acts, experimental acts, individual-case medicine preparation, and use aboard specified temporarily or accidentally present foreign conveyances.
Good-faith prior users (or serious preparers) before the filing or priority date may continue enterprise use within the patent territory; the right transfers only with the enterprise or business.

Government agencies or authorized third persons may exploit the invention without agreement for public-interest grounds (national security, nutrition, health, vital sectors) or adjudged anti-competitive exploitation, subject to Secs. 95-97 and 100-102 conditions.
All technology transfer arrangements must comply with the Chapter, whose policy is encouraging technology transfer while preventing or controlling IP abuses harming competition and trade.
Absent contrary agreement, licensing does not prevent the licensor from further licensing or self-exploitation.
The licensee may exploit the arrangement's subject matter during the whole arrangement term.

The Director of Legal Affairs may compulsorily license a capable exploiter on grounds including national emergency or extreme urgency, vital public interests, or adjudged anti-competitive exploitation.

Compulsory-license safeguards: purpose-limited scope and duration; non-exclusive; non-assignable except with the enterprise or goodwill; predominantly for the Philippine market (anti-competitive exception); termination when grounds cease and are unlikely to recur; and adequate patentee remuneration.
Patents and applications are assignable, inheritable, bequeathable and licensable; the written instrument must be recorded in the Office and is ineffective against third parties until recorded.

Unauthorized product or process acts constitute infringement. Civil relief: damages, attorney's fees, expenses, injunction; reasonable royalty where damages are unascertainable; up to triple damages; removal or destruction of infringing articles; and contributory liability for active inducement or knowing supply of specially adapted components.

Repetition of infringement after final judgment, by the infringer or connivers, is criminal: 6 months-3 years and/or P100,000-P300,000, without prejudice to civil damages. The action prescribes in three years from commission.

Literary and artistic works are original intellectual creations protected from creation: books and writings; periodicals; oral-delivery works; letters; dramatic, musical and choreographic works; art and applied art; maps, plans and technical works; photographs; audiovisual works; illustrations and ads; computer programs; and other literary, scholarly, scientific and artistic works - irrespective of expression mode, content, quality or purpose.

Exclusive economic rights, subject to Chapter VIII: reproduction; transformation (dramatization, translation, adaptation, abridgment, arrangement); first public distribution; rental of specified work types; public display; public performance; and other communication to the public.
Copyright vests automatically on creation, irrespective of expression mode, content, quality or purpose; deposit and notice are not conditions.

Derivative works (alterations of literary/artistic works; original collections and compilations) are protected as new works without affecting subsisting original-work copyright or implying use rights. Publishers hold only the typographical-arrangement reproduction right in the published edition.

No protection for ideas, procedures, systems, methods, concepts, principles, discoveries or mere data as such (even as embodied); day-to-day news and mere press items; or official legislative, administrative or legal texts and their official translations. Expression, not idea, is protected.

No copyright subsists in Philippine Government works, but commercial exploitation needs prior creating-agency approval and may incur royalties. GOCC works are separately registrable by the corporation. The Government may receive and hold transferred copyrights.
The author is the natural person who created the work; ownership may follow special employee, commissioned, joint and audiovisual rules.

Ownership: original works belong to the author; joint authors co-own (separable parts to their authors); employee creations outside regular duties belong to the employee, those from assigned duties to the employer absent agreement; commissioned works belong to the commissioner but copyright stays with the creator absent written stipulation otherwise; audiovisual copyright is shared per statute subject to producer exercise rights; letters belong to the writer under Civil Code Art. 723.

Publishers presumptively represent published authors and may sue for infringement. Anonymous and pseudonymous works run fifty years from first lawful publication; revealed identity invokes Sec. 213.1.

Terms: ordinary works life plus 50 years (posthumous included); joint works last-survivor life plus 50; anonymous/pseudonymous 50 years from first lawful publication (unpublished 50 from making); applied art 25 from making; photographic/audiovisual 50 from publication or making. Post-death/post-publication terms begin January 1 of the next year.
Copyright or exclusive-right owners may deposit two copies with the National Library (and law works with the Supreme Court Library) for record completion; deposit is not a protection condition.
Published or for-sale copies may bear a notice naming the owner and the first-publication year (plus death year for posthumous copies). Notice identifies; it does not create copyright.

Copyright is assignable or licensable in whole or part, with inter vivos transfers indicated in writing and exclusive licensees receiving in-scope rights and remedies; copyright is distinct from the material object; owners may transfer under the Act; and collective-management societies need IPO accreditation to enforce member rights.

Non-infringing acts (a)-(l): private free recitation/performance and qualifying charitable/religious use; justified attributed quotations; unreserved media use of lectures and current topics; current-events reporting; attributed teaching illustration; limited educational broadcast recordings; broadcasters' ephemeral recordings; qualifying public-interest institutional uses; nonprofit no-fee performances; specified public display; judicial/legal-advice use; and nonprofit specialized-format copies for the print-disabled. Each is conditional and must not conflict with normal exploitation or unreasonably prejudice legitimate interests.

Fair use for criticism, comment, news, teaching (including limited classroom copies), scholarship, research and similar purposes - plus qualifying interoperability decompilation - is not infringement. Four factors: purpose and character; work nature; amount and substantiality; market or value effect. Unpublished status alone does not bar fair use.
Secs. 184 and 186 preserve the Government's right to make or authorize translations, adaptations or publication of a work when necessary to its functions.

A natural person may make one private copy of a published work exclusively for research and private study, excluding building-form architecture, reprographic whole/substantial books and graphic musical works, data compilations, computer programs (except Sec. 189), and exploitation-conflicting reproduction.

Nonprofit libraries and archives may make limited mandate-necessary copies: fragile or rare works; isolated articles or brief research portions; and preservation or replacement of lost, destroyed or unusable publisher-unavailable copies.

Infringement by direct commission; knowing, controllable benefit from another's infringement; or knowing inducement, causation or material contribution. Relief: injunction; actual damages, costs, expenses and profits; statutory damages under the minimum and factors; increased technological-measure/RMI damages; and seizure or impounding of evidence.

Criminal penalties for infringement or aiding it: first offense 1-3 years and P50,000-P150,000; second 3 years 1 day-6 years and P150,000-P500,000; third and later 6 years 1 day-9 years and P500,000-P1,500,000. Maximum applies to specified technological-measure circumvention and RMI violations with knowing distribution, broadcast or communication.

Points of attachment: works (nationality, residence, headquarters, Philippine erection or first/30-day publication); performances (nationality, place, fixed or broadcast inclusion); sound recordings (producer nationality, first publication); and broadcasts (headquarters, transmitter situs).

Moral rights independent of economic rights: attribution; pre-publication alteration or withholding; objection to prejudicial distortion, mutilation, modification or derogatory action; and restraint of false or distorted name use.

No compelled creation or publication (damages for breach); written waiver allowed but never for false attribution or prejudicial name use; collective-work attribution deemed waived unless reserved; necessary publication-related editing is no violation; Sec. 193.1 attribution endures in perpetuity after death while 193.2-193.4 run with economic rights. Moral rights are unassignable and unlicensable.

Performers' exclusive authorization rights over live-performance broadcast and communication, fixation, and fixed-performance reproduction, distribution, rental and making available, plus identification and integrity moral rights - neighboring rights distinct from the underlying work's copyright.

Sound-recording producers' exclusive authorization rights over reproduction, first public distribution, commercial rental and making available, with related remuneration provisions - protecting the recording, not necessarily the underlying work.

Broadcasting organizations' exclusive rights over rebroadcasting, recording for public television communication, and fresh-transmission use of records - signal rights, not automatic rights in underlying works.
Chapter VIII copyright limitations apply mutatis mutandis to performers, sound-recording producers and broadcasting organizations.
